stem: The men in the image are laying tubes under a New York street in 1882. What larger change does this work show?

stimulus.source_note: Harper's Weekly, June 24, 1882, "The Electric Light in Houses — Laying the Tubes for Wires in the Streets of New York," drawn by W. P. Snyder. Public domain. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Laying_electric_lines_under_street_Edison_Pearl_Street_Utility_June_21_1882_Harpers_Weekly.png
stimulus.text: The image is a page from Harper's Weekly, June 24, 1882, titled "THE ELECTRIC LIGHT IN HOUSES — LAYING THE TUBES FOR WIRES IN THE STREETS OF NEW YORK." The top panel, "Laying the Electrical Tubes," shows workers digging a New York street and lowering thick tubes into the ground. The bottom panel, "Testing Tubes for Insulation," shows a worker at a tripod instrument and others handling coiled wire. An inset at the top right shows a worker pouring insulation.

options.text: Electricity was shifting from single machines to a central system that served whole neighborhoods
Every home had begun generating its own electricity with a private dynamo
options.misconception: Background: homes did not run their own dynamos; a central station made the power and sent it through wires to many customers.

options.text: New York had banned electricity, so the work was done in secret at night
options.misconception: Background: the work was public and celebrated in Harper's Weekly; the city welcomed the new light, it did not ban it.

options.text: Electric light had failed, and the men were digging the wires back up
options.misconception: Background: the men are laying new tubes, not removing old ones; the Pearl Street station opened weeks later, in September 1882.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Edison's Pearl Street station, opened in September 1882, was the first commercial power station in the United States, serving customers across about a square mile. The tubes in the street carried its power from one central station to many homes.
rationales.B: Background: a home dynamo would have been costly and dangerous. The whole point of the tubes was to bring power from one big station to many homes.
rationales.C: Background: Harper's Weekly pictured the work proudly in a full-page illustration inside the June 24, 1882 issue. The city did not ban the light; it dug its streets to welcome it.
rationales.D: Background: the men are laying tubes, not pulling them up, and the station opened in September 1882. The work was a beginning, not a cleanup.
rationales.general:
Ask where the power comes from: one place or many.
1. The tubes run under a whole street, not into a single house.
2. Background: they carried power from Edison's Pearl Street station, which served a whole square mile of customers at once.
3. Background: one central station feeding many homes is a system, not a gadget.
Remember: wires under a street mean power has left the workshop and become a utility.
